fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. For the unmarried and widows, Paul says, "It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am." He does talk about marrying in the very next verse, but that's for people who cannot control themselves. It's not an "as soon as you can" kind of thing.

Sitting together in the pew is a nice picture, friend, but that's not Paul's question. He asks, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" He asks the wife about her husband and the husband about his wife.

Right, baker. Paul asks, "Was a man already circumcised when he was called?" and answers, "He should not become uncircumcised." So he stays as he was when God called him. Paul says it again in verse 20: "Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called."

Traditions can feel very important, friend, but Paul doesn't use that word here. After saying circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing, he says, "Keeping God’s commandments is what counts." The word he gives is commandments, not traditions.

That's it, baker. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says it plainly: "…each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." He gives his reason right in the verse: there is so much sexual immorality. Notice he says "his own" and "her own."
Ha, that one would make for a hungry week, friend. But Paul doesn't set up any fasting day in this verse. What he says is that "…each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband."

You caught the "only," baker. Paul says, "The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband." That little word "likewise" puts the duty on both of them. It isn't just the husband's job.

Right on, baker. Paul says, "The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife." It goes both directions, and the "likewise" shows it. Neither one holds all the authority alone.
Neighbors, huh? Good guess, friend. But Paul doesn't blame the neighbors in this verse. He says to come together again "…so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control."

I see why "reward" sounds nice, friend, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says, "…each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that." It's a gift, and he says one person has this gift and another has that.

Customs aren't in this verse, friend. Paul's command, which he says is from the Lord and not from him, says, "A wife must not separate from her husband." Nothing in it mentions her keeping his customs.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy." So the children are holy, not unclean, just as the statement says. That makes it true.
